title: The Stool Test You Mail Back Cuts Death Risk by 43%
hook: Across 376,000 Swedes followed long-term, people who took part in colorectal cancer screening were 43% less likely to die of it. The test is one you do at home.
key_points: Long-term Swedish data on more than 376,000 people compared screening participants with non-participants.
Participants had a 43% lower risk of dying from colorectal cancer.
The screening entry point is a simple at-home stool test, not an immediate colonoscopy.
Screening works by finding cancers early and by catching precursor polyps before they turn.
The practical barrier is participation — an unreturned kit protects no one.
Colorectal cancer is one of the few common cancers with a well-validated, low-effort screen.
content_html: Screening studies rarely produce a number this clean. Following more than 376,000 people in Sweden over the long term, researchers found that those who took part in colorectal cancer screening had a 43% lower risk of dying from the disease than those who didn't.
extra_html:
What makes it worth a card is how little the participation costs. In programs like Sweden's, the front door isn't a colonoscopy — it's a stool test you do at home and send back, with follow-up scoping reserved for the results that warrant it. Colorectal cancer also gives screening an unusual double advantage: it can catch a tumor early, and it can catch the precursor polyp before there is a tumor at all.

The gap between the benefit and the reality is almost entirely behavioral. Invitations go out; kits go unreturned. If you're in the age range your local guidelines cover — and if you have a family history or symptoms like unexplained bleeding or a persistent change in bowel habits, regardless of age — this is the rare preventive step with a large, well-measured payoff and a very small ask. Sweden's program details differ from other countries', so ask your clinician what applies where you live.

related.title: Cancer Screenings Worth Knowing
related.hook: Screening looks for cancer before symptoms start — and for a few common cancers, that early catch dramatically improves the odds.

related.title: The Colon Cancer Warning Signs Young Adults Shrug Off
related.hook: Colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of cancer death in people under 50 — and it's still rising. A handful of symptoms are worth taking seriously long before the recommended screening age.

related.title: Why Regular Checkups Matter
related.hook: The whole point of a checkup is to catch trouble while it's still quiet — before symptoms show up and while it's easiest to treat.

related.title: One Blood Test for Many Cancers?
related.hook: A single blood draw that screens for many cancers at once could win FDA approval within months — a potential shift in how cancer gets caught early.

flashcards.prompt: How much lower was colorectal cancer death risk among screening participants?
flashcards.explanation_html: In long-term follow-up of more than 376,000 people in Sweden, participants in colorectal cancer screening had a 43% lower risk of dying from the disease than non-participants.

flashcards.prompt: Why does colorectal screening save lives in two different ways?
flashcards.back_html: It finds cancers early, when treatment works better — and it catches precursor polyps before they become cancer at all. Few screens do both.

flashcards.prompt: What is the practical bottleneck on this benefit?
flashcards.back_html: Participation. The entry test is a stool sample you collect at home and mail back; a kit that sits in a drawer delivers none of the 43%.
